## Kernel TCP/IP

## The Kernel Transmit Path

1. Copy application bytes into a kernel buffer.

2. Process TCP state and protocol headers.

3. Queue packet work and pass it to the driver.

4. Let the NIC fetch packet data with DMA.

5. Retain unacknowledged bytes for retransmission.

The user-to-kernel boundary copies the payload in this ordinary path.

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_1285_381_1676_1323.jpg" alt="Image" width="19%" /></div>

<!-- page: 8 -->

## Kernel TCP/IP

## The Kernel Receive Path

1. The NIC DMAs data into a kernel buffer.

2. An interrupt schedules receive processing.

3. NAPI, GRO, and TCP/IP process the data.

4. TCP makes ordered bytes available to the socket.

5. recv() copies bytes into the application buffer.

Packet arrival and application consumption are different events.

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_1117_381_1797_1323.jpg" alt="Image" width="34%" /></div>

<!-- page: 9 -->

## Kernel TCP/IP

## Interrupts and NAPI

## Receive processing

1. An IRQ schedules NAPI.

2. Poll work in batches, up to the receive budget.

3. When work is drained, complete NAPI and re-enable interrupts.

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_911_390_1897_1085.jpg" alt="Image" width="49%" /></div>


One interrupt can lead to processing multiple received packets.

Notification starts processing. DMA moves the packet bytes.

<!-- page: 10 -->

## Kernel TCP/IP

## TSO and GRO


<table border=1 style='margin: auto; word-wrap: break-word;'><tr><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Mechanism</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Description</td></tr><tr><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>TSO (Tx)</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>TCP Segmentation Offload. Offloads the segmentation of “big” packets (up to 64KB) into frames to the NIC.</td></tr><tr><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>GRO (Rx)</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Generic Receive Offload. Aggregates MTU-sized frames into a “big” packet (up to 64KB) before passing them to the TCP/IP layer.</td></tr></table>

GSO provides software segmentation. TSO delegates it to the NIC. GRO combines received segments before TCP processing.

Larger processing units amortize protocol and buffer-management work.

Wire packets still obey the MTU. Receive aggregation happens at the host.

## Packet Processing at 100 Gb/s

### 100 Gb/s = 12.5 GB/s nominal link rate


<table border=1 style='margin: auto; word-wrap: break-word;'><tr><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Ethernet frame</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Wire occupancy</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Packet rate</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Cycles/frame</td></tr><tr><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>64 B</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>84 byte-times</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>148.8 Mpps</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>20.2</td></tr><tr><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>1518 B</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>1538 byte-times</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>8.13 Mpps</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>369.1</td></tr></table>

Add 8 B preamble/SFD and 12 byte-times of inter-frame gap.

Cycles/frame = 3 GHz / packet rate, for one idealized CPU core.

Calculated at 100 Gb/s. Nominal MAC rate, before payload and processing overheads.

Small packets leave very little CPU work per frame.

- Actual throughput also depends on memory, queueing, and offloads.

## Scale-Up Networks

## Design Requirements for a Scale-Up Domain

A scale-up domain needs bandwidth, reliable paths, and correct completion.

Three design questions

Endpoint: how many bytes can each device inject?

Fabric: which paths will carry those bytes?

Software: when may the receiver consume them?

## Full copper

Short reach

Dense rack cabling

Lower optics cost

## Copper + optics

Longer reach

Additional switch tier

More complex paths

## Full optical

Across racks, one tier

Higher optics cost / power

NPO or pluggable LPO

EtherNode chooses optical reach to preserve a flat fabric.

## Middleware Layer: Buffers and QP Resources

The Network Abstraction Layer manages buffers, mappings, and QPs.

GPU / rank channels

NAL: buffer + QP pool

Leased QP / path bundles

Static full-path provisioning

## 32 local GPUs × 511 peers × 16 paths = 261,632 QP contexts

Available per rack

65,536 QPs

Allocate paths on demand. Reclaim only after outstanding work drains.

Unified buffer management is a software abstraction, not cache-coherent shared HBM.

## Scale-Up Networks

## EtherNode: Summary of Design Choices

Scaling accelerator and memory domains over commodity Ethernet


<table border=1 style='margin: auto; word-wrap: break-word;'><tr><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Design constraint</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Our design choice</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Why this choice</td></tr><tr><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Limited physical reach</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Full optical I/O</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Extend connectivity across racks while preserving a single-tier fabric</td></tr><tr><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>High bandwidth under a tight I/O-die budget</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Multi-plane, single-hop fabric with fixed per-QP paths</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Aggregate bandwidth while reducing packet-reordering buffer requirements</td></tr><tr><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Cross-path ordering and finite connection resources</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Software transaction module and shared resource pools</td><td style='text-align: center; word-wrap: break-word;'>Coordinate completion and ordering. Allocate QPs and buffers on demand.</td></tr></table>

Optical reach adds cost and power. Software carries cross-path semantics and resource management.

A scale-up network combines high-bandwidth connectivity with explicit transfer semantics and resource management.
